title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
hook: a scholar lost his voice and his certainty, left his post, and found his way through Sufi practice

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was muraqaba: keeping watch over the heart, and knowing you are seen. Your line was watchful.

A teacher stands up to lecture, and his tongue won't move. That's how Abu Hamid al-Ghazali tells it, in a short account of his own life called Deliverance from Error. He was teaching in Baghdad, with students in front of him, and his tongue dried up so that he could not teach. Grief took hold of him. He could hardly eat or swallow. The doctors examined him and gave up; the trouble, they said, wasn't in his body. It had settled in his heart.
screen: `A TONGUE THAT WOULD NOT MOVE.` → `THE DOCTORS GAVE UP.` → `IT HAD SETTLED IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: The trouble began earlier, in his mind. He wanted certain knowledge, the kind that leaves no room for doubt, so he tested what he knew. The senses? The eye sees a shadow standing still, yet it moves. It sees a star as small as a coin, yet reasoning shows it is vast. If reason corrects the senses, what corrects reason? Perhaps a higher judge would show reason up, the way waking shows up a dream. He fell into a doubt that argument couldn't cure, since every argument is built out of the very things in doubt. Then, he says, he was healed: not by arranging proofs, but by a light that God cast into his breast. The second crisis came later. Now he had answers, but his life didn't match them. Looking honestly, he saw how much of his teaching was driven by wanting to be known. He wavered between the pull of the world and the call to leave it, until, as he tells it, the choice was made for him, and his tongue stopped. In the end he left Baghdad, gave up his post, and went seeking solitude and the practice of the Sufis. What he found there, he says, couldn't be learned only from books. It had to be tasted. Knowing the definition of health, he writes, is not the same as being healthy. Neither time, by his own account, did the way through come from a better argument.
screen: `THE SHADOW AND THE STAR.` · `A LIGHT CAST INTO THE BREAST.` · `LEAVING THE POST.` · `TASTED, NOT ONLY KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question in your life that won't resolve, a choice, a doubt, something you keep turning over, and don't work on it now; al-Ghazali couldn't argue his way out, so for these minutes, don't argue. Set it down beside you like a heavy bag and rest: if you pray, you can hand it to God, and if you don't, simply leave it there and breathe. If a weight like his is on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency number.
Al-Ghazali's crisis. A scholar's doubt, a tongue that would not move, and a way through found by tasting Sufi practice, not by proof. Today's word.
Your line: lost, then found. Some knowing can only be tasted, never just argued into. Take care.

howItsDone: Al-Ghazali's Deliverance from Error is read as a spiritual autobiography in Islamic thought; Muslims and others turn to it as an account of doubt, of the limits of argument, and of finding a way through Sufi practice.

notes: All of Deliverance from Error is paraphrased (Claud Field's 1909 translation exists but is not on the validator list and its wording was not checked). Confirm each beat: the search for certain knowledge; the shadow and the star examples; the dream analogy; the doubt cured 'not by arranging proofs' but by 'a light God cast into the breast'; teaching in Baghdad; recognizing the desire for reputation; wavering between the world and leaving; the tongue drying up, inability to eat, doctors saying the matter was in the heart; leaving his post for solitude and Sufi practice; dhawq (tasting) and the health/definition analogy.
The script gives no dates, ages, number of students or length of travel, under the claims rule. The index hook's 'famous scholar' was softened to 'a scholar'.
